analysis.one_liner: Lets supplement makers advertise disease-related health claims without FDA drug approval.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the food and drug law so that foods, including dietary supplements, are no longer legally considered drugs. That would let supplement makers tell customers a product affects a disease or health condition without running the clinical trials and FDA review that drug makers must run. It also loosens the safety standard so the FDA could only pull a risky supplement off the market if its danger is both significant and unreasonable, a harder test than the current one. The bill died quietly in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Dietary supplement makers gain the most. Today, if a supplement claims to treat or prevent a disease, it is regulated as a drug and needs FDA approval backed by testing. Excluding all food and supplements from the drug definition removes that hurdle, letting companies make disease-related health claims without proving they work or are safe. The softer "significant and unreasonable" safety standard also makes it harder for the FDA to recall a dangerous ingredient.

how_it_helps.text: Excludes food, including dietary supplements, from the legal definition of a "drug," so supplements with disease-related claims would no longer need FDA drug approval.

Raises the bar for FDA action by replacing the "significant or unreasonable" risk test with "significant and unreasonable," meaning a supplement could pose a serious risk and still stay on the market if that risk were judged reasonable.
Sponsors framed the change as free speech for health information, arguing that consumers should be able to hear claims about the health benefits of foods and supplements.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers bear the cost: they would see disease-related claims on supplement labels that never had to be proven in clinical trials, and dangerous ingredients could stay on shelves longer because the FDA would face a stricter test to remove them. Drug makers also face cheaper, unproven competition for health conditions their products treat.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets supplement makers make disease-related claims without running clinical trials or getting FDA approval, so consumers could spend money on products whose claimed benefits are unproven.

Changing the removal standard from "significant or unreasonable" to "significant and unreasonable" risk means a supplement could present a serious health risk and remain legal if the FDA deemed that risk reasonable.

Supporters would argue the current rules deny consumers truthful information about foods and supplements; the counterargument is that claims about treating disease have historically required proof precisely because consumers rely on them when making health decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is more health information on supplement labels; its cost is that none of that information would have to be proven, and the FDA would have a harder time removing genuinely dangerous ingredients. For a product category people take for their health, removing the proof requirement shifts the risk onto consumers. The bill's modest cosponsor list (9) and quick death in committee suggest even its supporters saw limited prospects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ron Paul introduced the bill on March 11, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce.
On March 30, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where no further action was taken.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept the existing rule that disease-related claims require drug-level testing and that the FDA can act when a supplement presents a significant OR unreasonable risk. Supplement makers gained nothing, and drug makers faced no new unproven competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and the FDA's current standards

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was small and bipartisan — 7 Republicans, 1 Democrat, and 1 Independent among 9 cosponsors — and with no hearings or votes, the record shows no organized opposition either way.

industries.note: The bill would free supplement makers to make disease-related claims without clinical trials or FDA approval, opening a larger marketing space than current law allows. The gain comes from removing proof requirements that exist to protect consumers relying on health claims.

Supplements could be marketed against drugs treating the same conditions without ever being tested, cutting into prescription and over-the-counter drug markets. In this bill, the drug industry's interest in keeping claim-proof requirements runs alongside the public's interest in tested products.
Consumers would hear more claims about supplement benefits, but none would have to be proven, and dangerous ingredients would be harder for the FDA to remove.
